title: Testing Ecological Cause in the Field
endLine: Randomly change one factor against matched controls to test ecological cause.

scenes.tts: One hillside of grass grows lush while another stays sparse. Why? Two real sites differ in soil, slope, rain, and history all at once. Watching nature alone cannot separate those tangled factors. A field manipulation experiment tests cause by changing one factor inside one place.
scenes.caption: One hillside of grass grows lush while another stays sparse. Why? Two real sites differ in soil, slope, rain, and history all at once. Watching nature alone cannot separate those tangled factors. A field manipulation experiment tests cause by changing one factor inside one place.
scenes.visual: Split-screen view of two swaying grassland hillsides (schematic): the left is thick and green, the right is sparse and pale, with a bold question mark rising between them. As soil, slope, rain, and history are named, distinct soil layers, slope angles, falling raindrops, and subtle timeline icons animate and tangle together between the sites; then the split dissolves to focus on one hillside.
scenes.narration: One hillside of grass grows lush while another stays sparse. Why? Two real sites differ in soil, slope, rain, and history all at once. Watching nature alone cannot separate those tangled factors. A field manipulation experiment tests cause by changing one factor inside one place.

scenes.visual: The camera zooms smoothly into the single uniform grassland hillside as grass ripples gently in the wind (schematic). The title "Testing Ecological Cause in the Field" fades in at center and fades out cleanly.

scenes.tts: Inside that one grassland, divide the slope into matched blocks with similar soil. Within each block, mark equal plots and flip a coin. Some plots receive the treatment; untouched plots serve as controls. Choosing by eye could pick the healthiest spots. Random assignment removes that bias and balances hidden differences on average.

scenes.visual: The same grassland hillside divides horizontally along elevation bands into matched blocks (schematic), each sharing one soil tone. Equal rectangular plots draw inside each block. A brief ghost hand reaches toward the greenest plots and is crossed out; instead a spinning coin flips over each pair of plots, lighting treated plots in a bright accent colour and leaving matched control plots untouched, while subtle soil-variation speckles even out across groups (schematic).
scenes.narration: Inside that one grassland, divide the slope into matched blocks with similar soil. Within each block, mark equal plots and flip a coin. scenes.tts: Now change one factor while keeping plot area alike. You can remove a species, or add a resource like water or light. Or build an exclosure: a cage or shelter that keeps one influence out. To test cause in nature, change one factor at random while matched controls hold everything else alike.

scenes.visual: Three treated plots inside the same grassland blocks animate in sequence while their paired control plots stay unchanged beside them (schematic): on the first, selected plant stems lift out to show removal; on the second, droplets and light rays enter to show addition; on the third, a translucent mesh cage and a clear shelter frame lower over the grass to show an exclosure. Matched control borders glow steadily beside each manipulated plot.

scenes.tts: Picture rain-out shelters built over those grassland plots. Roofs block natural rain. Irrigation then returns the same total, either in the natural pattern or as fewer, larger storms. Yet each roof stays over the grass all season. What side effect could mislead you, and what extra control plot checks for it?

scenes.visual: Camera zooms in on two plots in the same grassland, each covered by a slanted rain-out roof (schematic). Natural rain bounces off both roofs while irrigation nozzles underneath deliver equal total water: gentle, frequent showers on the left plot and fewer, heavy bursts on the right (schematic). A sun arc rises overhead as the roofs remain in place and the question "What else does the roof change? What extra plot checks?" appears at top.

scenes.visual: Hold the question "What else does the roof change? What extra plot checks?" on screen above the two sheltered grassland plots (schematic). Sunlight drifts slowly across the shelter roofs, casting a faint shadow beneath while grass blades sway gently.

scenes.tts: A shelter can cast shade and warm the air beneath it. So experimenters add unsheltered plots to check whether the roof itself changed plant growth. They also log soil moisture to confirm the treatment made moisture more variable. Cage exclosures need a similar check: report how well the mesh actually kept predators out.

scenes.visual: Under the same rain-out roofs, a cool shadow deepens and warm rising shimmer lines appear (schematic: possible side effects, not measured). An open, unsheltered grassland plot slides into the same block beside them for comparison. Beneath the soil line, a schematic moisture trace draws steady ripples under natural timing and wide swings under fewer, larger storms. At the block's edge, a small mesh cage highlights its weave as a predator icon tests the barrier (schematic).

scenes.tts: Even careful controls have limits. With only one treated block, chance differences can mimic a real effect, so treatments must be replicated. One unusual year of weather can also dominate, so plots are tracked for several years. And a field result applies to that site first; another grassland or shore can respond differently.

scenes.visual: The camera pulls back to show a single block flickering ambiguously, then multiplies into several replicated blocks across the grassland hillside (schematic). A schematic year counter advances across four growing seasons while cloud and sun icons vary each year. Finally, a faint outline of a second landscape—another grassland and a rocky shore—appears beside the field with a subtle question mark (schematic).

scenes.tts: These designs unlocked real causes. In 2002, Knapp and colleagues ran those shelters for four years in a grassland with moderate rain. Fewer, larger events raised soil-moisture variability, lowered plant growth, and raised species diversity. Fertilized experimental grassland communities lose species. In 2009, Hautier, Niklaus, and Hector added light to their understory. That prevented the loss, pointing to competition for light.

scenes.visual: Two side-by-side panels stay inside the same grassland world (schematic). Left panel ("Knapp and colleagues, 2002"): rain-out shelter plots tick across four years; under fewer, larger rain bursts, a schematic moisture line swings wider, grass height drops slightly, and more distinct flower shapes appear. Right panel ("Hautier, Niklaus and Hector, 2009"): fertilizer granules drop onto dense grass, shading out short species in fertilized plots without added light, while an understory lamp in fertilized plots with added light keeps short species alive.

In 2009, Hautier, Niklaus, and Hector added light to their understory. That prevented the loss, pointing to competition for light.

scenes.tts: In 1997, Andrew Beckerman, Maria Uriarte, and Oswald Schmitz tested grasshoppers in a Connecticut old field. They compared enclosures with no spiders, hunting spiders, or spiders with glued mouthparts that could not kill. Any effect of glued spiders could only come from fear, not killing. By changing one factor at random beside matched controls, field manipulations turn tangled patterns into testable causes.

Camera then pulls smoothly back over the full replicated field as treated and matched control plots glow cleanly together (schematic).
